descriptor.scene: A quiet moment. A view down the length of the working line with FIVE COMPLETELY DIFFERENT PAPER PLANES sitting at five different points along the bench, one at each machine, waiting their turn: a long thin dart, a short fat one, a broad square-ish one, one with upturned wingtips, and one blunt-nosed. They could not look less like each other and the line is treating them all exactly the same. Mira stands at the near end with her hands at her sides, just looking at it, calm and a little brave about it. Soft daylight from the four-pane window. No other people. THERE IS NO ROBOT, NO MECHANICAL FIGURE, NO TOY ROBOT, NO AUTOMATON and NO MACHINE WITH A FACE anywhere in this image. Only the people named above are present.

prompt: Picture-book spread painted in the warm editorial ink-and-wash register of the FIRST reference image. THE FIRST REFERENCE IMAGE IS A STYLE ANCHOR ONLY. Match it for MEDIUM, BRUSHWORK, PALETTE and LIGHT QUALITY ONLY, and take NO subject from it whatsoever: none of its objects, figures, costume, props, furniture, architecture, period or location may appear in the output unless the scene description below asks for them by name. WARM EDITORIAL INK-AND-WASH illustration: a loose confident ink line with soft transparent watercolour washes over it, a muted earth palette of cream, rust, ochre, mustard, sage and warm grey, quiet and hand-made, the look of a thoughtful printed picture book. It is NOT neon, NOT 3D or CGI or Pixar, NOT glossy plastic, NOT neo-comic, and carries NO HUD or arc-reactor comic vocabulary. ONE single full-bleed scene per image: never a grid, never split panels, never a contact sheet, never a before-and-after. This is a children's picture book about building a little factory in a garden shed that will make any paper plane at all, so long as it flies. Each spread contains ONLY the figures its own scene description names. Keep the LOWER RIGHT of the frame calm and uncluttered, because a caption card sits there. SCENE: A quiet moment. A view down the length of the working line with FIVE COMPLETELY DIFFERENT PAPER PLANES sitting at five different points along the bench, one at each machine, waiting their turn: a long thin dart, a short fat one, a broad square-ish one, one with upturned wingtips, and one blunt-nosed. They could not look less like each other and the line is treating them all exactly the same. Mira stands at the near end with her hands at her sides, just looking at it, calm and a little brave about it. Soft daylight from the four-pane window. No other people. THERE IS NO ROBOT, NO MECHANICAL FIGURE, NO TOY ROBOT, NO AUTOMATON and NO MACHINE WITH A FACE anywhere in this image. Only the people named above are present. mira rendered exactly per the supplied reference images: a girl about ten ordinary not precocious; dark hair in a blunt chin length bob with a straight fringe; mustard yellow knitted cardigan over a plain rust red dress; bare knees and scuffed cream canvas shoes; hands are always doing something folding holding throwing; warm editorial ink and wash never photoreal. MIRA, a girl of about TEN. Dark hair in a blunt CHIN-LENGTH BOB with a straight fringe across her forehead. A MUSTARD-YELLOW KNITTED CARDIGAN, sleeves pushed up, over a plain RUST-RED DRESS. Bare knees. Scuffed CREAM CANVAS SHOES. She is an ORDINARY CHILD, absorbed and a bit stubborn, NOT precocious, NOT a prodigy, NOT tidy. Her hands are always occupied. Warm-editorial ink-and-wash on a cream ground, soft washes over a loose ink line, never photoreal, never 3D, never glossy. CONVERGENCE IS THE FAILURE MODE. Any render in which the planes read as copies of one handsome dart has argued against the book and must be regenerated from scratch, not accepted and not patched. This applies hardest on the final spread, where a hundred planes must read as a hundred designs. the-plane-shed exactly as its reference plate: THE PLANE SHED: an ordinary small backyard timber shed a child could actually have, roughly three metres by four. Weathered grey-brown VERTICAL BOARD walls and a LOW SINGLE-PITCH ROOF sloping down toward the yard, low enough that a child on an upturned crate can climb onto it. The door is in the SHORT wall facing the yard. ONE SQUARE FOUR-PANE WINDOW sits in the LONG wall, with a WORKBENCH running the full length of that wall beneath it. Shelves and a pegboard above the bench. A single bare bulb on a flex. Outside the door, a LOW CONCRETE STEP of two treads; beyond it a mown grass yard about fifteen metres long ending in a WAIST-HIGH WOODEN GATE, which is the far marker the first plane reaches. NEVER a laboratory, NEVER a factory floor, NEVER a maker-space, NEVER impressive. HANDEDNESS IS FIXED AND NEVER CHANGES BETWEEN SPREADS, and this is the single most important rule about this room. In EVERY interior view, without exception: the OPEN DOORWAY is at the LEFT-HAND END of the room with green grass and daylight beyond it; the WORKBENCH runs along the RIGHT-HAND wall, receding away from the doorway; the SQUARE FOUR-PANE WINDOW is in that same right-hand wall, directly ABOVE the bench; the SHELVES and the PEGBOARD are above and beyond the bench on that right-hand wall; the single BARE BULB hangs from the ceiling near the middle. The THROWING ARM, once it exists, is always clamped at the bench end NEAREST THE DOORWAY, which is the LEFT end. The camera may come closer or pull wider, and may stand anywhere in the room, BUT IT NEVER CROSSES THE ROOM'S AXIS: the doorway is never on the right, the bench and window are never on the left, and the room is never mirrored. It is a SMALL room, three metres by four, and the ceiling is barely above an adult's head. The shed is CLUTTERED, WOODEN and WARM, and everything in it is plainly hand-made by children: loose sheets of paper, a jar of pencils, blunt scissors, string, pencil marks straight on the bench top, folded paper planes lying where they were put down. Light is only daylight through the four-pane window plus one bare bulb; never dramatic, never rim-lit, never moody. RENDER ONE MOMENT IN TIME ONLY: a single view of the shed as it is in this one scene, never a before-and-after, never a split panel, never two versions of the room in one image. Small enough that two children fill it. A viewer must believe two kids built everything in the room. Pip is a small tin toy no taller than a child's knee and is NEVER as tall as the workbench. NEGATIVES: neon, 3D/CGI/Pixar, glossy plastic, HUD/arc-reactor comic vocabulary, neo-comic, NO STRAY OR INVENTED TEXT anywhere: no captions, no labels, no signage, no watermarks, no logos, no signatures, no dates, no readable handwriting and no readable print. THE ONE EXCEPTION is text a scene specifies as an exact quoted string., NO ADULTS anywhere in this book: no parents, no teacher, no crowd. Only the two children and the helper., NO GLOWING TECHNOLOGY: no screens, no displays, no dials with readouts, no holograms, no blue light, no cables, no motors, no chrome, no sleek modern product design. Every machine is hand-made from scrap wood, tin, wire and spring steel., NO PLANE MAY BE A COPY OF ANOTHER: wherever more than one paper plane appears in a frame, every one of them must be a VISIBLY DIFFERENT FOLD. A tidy squadron of matching darts is a failure of the whole book., NO character may be lit from below, haloed, or gazed up at., PIP IS NEVER LARGER THAN KNEE-HIGH to Mira and never dominates a frame.. ONE SINGLE CONTINUOUS FULL-BLEED PAINTING that fills the entire canvas edge to edge. This is NEVER a grid, NEVER a multi-panel layout, NEVER a comic page, NEVER a contact sheet, NEVER a study or turnaround sheet, NEVER a collage, and NEVER several framed views side by side. Some reference images supplied to you are multi-panel study sheets; use them ONLY for the identity and design of what they depict, and NEVER copy their panelled layout into the output. The output has exactly ONE camera, ONE moment, and NO internal borders, frames, gutters, or dividing lines of any kind.
